title: Great Books · Episode 2
chapters: Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction
Alice in Wonderland: the story told on a river

units.t: Great Books. Episode two.
In this episode: The rise of the novel, Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction, Charles Dickens and the cliffhanger and Alice in Wonderland: the story told on a river.
Part one. The rise of the novel.
The novel is the youngest of the great literary forms, yet it became the way billions of people explore other lives.
Here's how it began, and the Australian books worth knowing.
The first novels.
A novel is a long, invented story told in prose, usually focused on characters' inner lives.
The word comes from the Italian 'novella', meaning a new story.
Around AD 1000 in Japan, the court lady Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, a subtle story of life at the imperial court.
It is often called the world's first novel, though 'first' depends on how strictly you define the form.
In Europe, the book most often called the first modern novel is Cervantes' Don Quixote, 1605 and 1615.
A gentleman reads so many chivalry tales that he becomes a knight and attacks windmills, believing them giants.
It gave English the word 'quixotic' and the phrase 'tilting at windmills'.
English novels take off.
Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, 1719, is often called the first English novel.
It presented itself as a true account of a sailor shipwrecked for 28 years, and its power came from practical detail.
Defoe was probably partly inspired by Alexander Selkirk, marooned off Chile from 1704 to 1709.
Richardson's Pamela, 1740, and Fielding's Tom Jones, 1749, followed.
The novel spread because several changes arrived together: cheaper printing, rising literacy, and a middle class with money and leisure.
Circulating libraries let readers borrow books for a fee, and many readers and writers were women.
Unlike epics about heroes, novels focused on ordinary people.
The form proved flexible, producing Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, 1818, an early science fiction work.
Austen and Dickens.
Jane Austen, 1775–1817, published four novels in her lifetime, all anonymously, the first credited only to 'a Lady'.
Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared after her death at 41.
Pride and Prejudice, 1813, opens with the famous line about a single man in possession of a good fortune.
She wrote about courtship, class and money with sharp irony, and refined a way of slipping in and out of a character's thoughts.
Charles Dickens, 1812–1870, was Victorian England's superstar novelist.
At 12, when his father was jailed for debt, he worked in a boot polish factory, an experience that fuelled his anger at poverty.
Most of his novels came out in weekly or monthly instalments, much like a TV series.
'Dickensian' now describes grim, overcrowded poverty.
Australia's classics.
Australian novels grew out of the colonial experience.
Marcus Clarke's For the Term of His Natural Life, first serialised in the early 1870s, told a harrowing story of the convict system.
Dickens's Great Expectations also features a convict transported to New South Wales.
Miles Franklin's My Brilliant Career, 1901, about a spirited young woman in the bush, was written when she was very young, and her bequest later funded the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
Henry Handel Richardson was the pen name of Ethel Richardson, author of The Getting of Wisdom.
Patrick White, author of Voss and The Tree of Man, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973.
He was the first Australian to win it.
Modern Australian voices.
Tim Winton has won the Miles Franklin Award four times.
His novel Cloudstreet, 1991, about two working-class families sharing a big old house in Perth, is often voted a favourite Australian book.
Kate Grenville's The Secret River, 2005, follows a convict settler on the Hawkesbury River and confronts the violence of colonisation.
Kim Scott, a Noongar writer, became the first Aboriginal author to win the Miles Franklin, for Benang in 2000.
Waanyi writer Alexis Wright won it for Carpentaria in 2007.
To start reading, pick one classic and one modern novel, and try your local library's free audiobook and ebook apps.
The key idea: The novel is long prose fiction about characters' inner lives, with early landmarks in Japan's Tale of Genji and Spain's Don Quixote.
Part two. Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction.
A teenager, a stormy summer and a ghost story contest produced one of the most influential novels ever written.
The year without summer.
In April 1815, Mount Tambora in what is now Indonesia exploded in one of the largest eruptions in recorded history.
Its ash and gases cooled the global climate, and Europe's 1816 became the year without a summer, with cold, rain and failed harvests.

That June, a group of young English writers stayed near Lake Geneva: the poet Lord Byron at the Villa Diodati, and nearby Percy Bysshe Shelley, eighteen-year-old Mary Godwin, her stepsister Claire Clairmont and Byron's doctor, John Polidori.
Trapped indoors, they read ghost stories aloud, and Byron proposed that each write one.
Mary struggled for days.
Polidori's effort became The Vampyre in 1819, which helped shape the vampire as an elegant aristocrat.
A waking dream.
After listening to Byron and Percy discuss whether life could be artificially created, Mary had what she later called a waking dream.
She pictured a pale student kneeling beside a thing he had put together, watching it stir into life, then fleeing in horror.
She described this in an introduction to the 1831 edition, so it is her own account, years later.
Mary was the daughter of two radical thinkers: Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, who died shortly after her birth, and the philosopher William Godwin.
Frankenstein was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was twenty.
Many reviewers assumed the author was a man.
Science at life's edge.
Frankenstein was not pure fantasy.
In the 1780s, the Italian scientist Luigi Galvani made the legs of dead frogs twitch using electricity, which led to the term galvanism.
His nephew Giovanni Aldini went further.
In London in 1803, he applied electric currents to the body of an executed criminal, making the face grimace and a hand rise, to the alarm of onlookers.
Many people wondered whether electricity might be the spark of life itself.
Mary Shelley knew about these debates.
In the novel, Victor Frankenstein is deliberately vague about his methods, but a scientist using cutting-edge knowledge to cross a forbidden line came straight from the science of her day.
The creature speaks.
Anyone who knows Frankenstein only from films may be surprised by the book.
First, Frankenstein is the scientist, Victor.
The creature is never given a name.
Second, he is no grunting brute.
Abandoned by his horrified creator, he teaches himself to speak and read by secretly watching a family through a gap in a cottage wall.
He reads Milton's Paradise Lost and compares himself to both Adam and Satan.
When he confronts Victor, he speaks with great eloquence about his loneliness and the cruelty he has suffered, and asks Victor to make him a companion.
Victor's refusal sets off the tragic final events.
The real horror of the book is rejection.
First science fiction.
Frankenstein grew out of the Gothic tradition of haunted castles, which began with Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764.
But Mary Shelley did something new.
Her monster was made not by a curse or spell but by a scientist using knowledge and method.
The writer Brian Aldiss argued this makes it the first true science fiction novel, a view many critics share.
The subtitle, The Modern Prometheus, points to the myth of the Titan who stole fire from the gods.
Her question was new: what responsibility do creators have for what they make?
The 1931 Universal film with Boris Karloff, and Jack Pierce's flat-topped makeup, turned the creature into a mostly silent icon.
The key idea: Frankenstein began in 1816, when a volcanic eruption's cold, stormy summer trapped young writers indoors.
Part three. Charles Dickens and the cliffhanger.
Dickens wrote his novels a few chapters at a time, while readers waited for each new instalment.
A secret childhood trauma shaped much of what he wrote.
The boy in the factory.
Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth in 1812, the son of a navy pay clerk who was hopeless with money.
In 1824, when Charles was twelve, his father was imprisoned for debt in London's Marshalsea prison, and much of the family moved in with him, as was common then.
Charles was sent to work in a warehouse near the Thames, pasting labels onto pots of boot blacking for about ten hours a day.
The job lasted perhaps a year, but he felt abandoned and humiliated.
He told almost no one.
The full story became public only after his death, when his friend John Forster published his biography.
The echoes run through his novels, which are full of orphans, debtors and cruel institutions.
Reporter to Pickwick.
Dickens had little formal schooling, but he taught himself shorthand and became a fast, skilled reporter, including in the press gallery of parliament.
He watched people closely and listened to how they spoke.
His humorous sketches of London life appeared under the pen name Boz.
In 1836 a publisher asked him to write text to accompany a series of comic sporting illustrations.
Dickens took control of the project, which became The Pickwick Papers.
Sales started slowly, but when the witty Cockney servant Sam Weller appeared, the story took off.
By the end of its run, each monthly part was selling tens of thousands of copies.
Dickens was in his mid-twenties and already the most popular author in Britain.
The serial machine.
Most of Dickens's novels first appeared in parts rather than as complete books.
The typical format was a monthly instalment of about 32 pages with two illustrations, costing one shilling, usually running for nineteen or twenty months.
Some novels, such as Oliver Twist, ran in magazines.
This made fiction affordable for more people, since buying a part a month was easier than paying for a whole book.
It also shaped how Dickens wrote.
He often stayed only a few instalments ahead of publication, ended parts on moments of suspense and could adjust stories in response to readers' reactions.
Families and neighbours gathered to read new instalments aloud, so a single copy might reach many listeners.
Little Nell and Christmas.
The Old Curiosity Shop, published weekly in 1840 and 1841, followed the doomed child Little Nell.
As her death approached, readers begged Dickens to spare her.
A famous story says crowds on a New York wharf shouted to arriving ships asking whether she was dead, but historians note the tale is poorly documented and may be embellished.
What is certain is that many readers grieved openly.
In 1843, short of money, Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks.
He insisted on an expensive edition with gilt edges and colour illustrations at a low price, so his profits disappointed.
The story helped popularise a Christmas of family, generosity and feasting.
He also fought piracy.
American publishers could reprint British books without paying the author, and the United States did not protect foreign authors meaningfully until 1891.
Readings and Staplehurst.
From the late 1850s, Dickens gave paid public readings of his work, playing every character with different voices and gestures.
Audiences in Britain and America packed halls to see him.
The tours earned him a fortune but exhausted him, especially his violent reading of the murder of Nancy from Oliver Twist.
In June 1865 he survived a serious railway accident at Staplehurst in Kent, when his train crashed on a bridge under repair.
He helped tend the injured and dying, then remembered his manuscript and climbed back into the carriage to retrieve it.
He was shaken for the rest of his life.
He died in 1870, five years to the day after the crash, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.
The key idea: A painful childhood spent pasting labels in a warehouse gave Dickens a lifelong sympathy for poor children.
Part four. Alice in Wonderland: the story told on a river.
On a summer afternoon in 1862, a shy maths lecturer made up a story to entertain three bored girls in a rowing boat.
It became one of the most translated books ever written.
A story made up aloud.
On 4 July 1862, Charles Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford, rowed up the Thames towards Godstow.
With him were his friend Robinson Duckworth and the three daughters of the college dean, Henry Liddell: Lorina, Alice and Edith.
Alice was ten.
To pass the time, Dodgson spun a tale about a girl named Alice who tumbles down a rabbit hole into a world where nothing behaves sensibly.
Duckworth later remembered asking if he was inventing it on the spot, and Dodgson said yes.
At the end of the day, Alice Liddell asked him to write it down for her.
He took the request seriously, though it took him more than two years to finish.
From gift to book.
Dodgson wrote the story out by hand, added his own pen drawings, and in November 1864 gave Alice a small volume titled Alice's Adventures Under Ground.
Friends who read it, including the writer George MacDonald, whose children loved it, urged him to publish.
He expanded the tale, adding episodes such as the Mad Tea-Party and the Cheshire Cat.
He also built a pen name from his own: Charles Lutwidge became Carolus Ludovicus, then was reversed and anglicised into Lewis Carroll.
He hired John Tenniel, the leading cartoonist of Punch, and paid for the illustrations himself.
Alice's Adventures in Wonderland appeared from Macmillan in 1865, and Tenniel's drawings have shaped how readers picture Alice ever since.
The edition that was recalled.
Tenniel was unhappy with the first printing of 2,000 copies in 1865, complaining that the pictures were badly printed.
Dodgson agreed to withdraw the edition and pay for a new one.
The reprint, dated 1866, is the edition most Victorian readers knew.
Many unbound sheets from the rejected run were sold to an American publisher and issued in the United States.
The few bound copies already given away became extreme rarities.
Only around two dozen copies of the original 1865 edition are known to survive, mostly in libraries, and one can sell for well over a million dollars at auction.
A perfectionist's fussing over ink and paper created one of the most sought-after books in the world.
Nonsense with rules.
Wonderland feels chaotic, but much of its humour is logic pushed to ridiculous extremes, as you might expect from a mathematician.
Characters take words literally, argue over definitions and follow rules that make no sense.
Many of Alice's poems parody the moralising verses Victorian children had to memorise.
The Hatter asks why a raven is like a writing desk and admits he has no idea.
For years Carroll gave no answer, and only in a later edition did he suggest a playful one.
The book never actually calls him the Mad Hatter.
He is simply the Hatter, though the Cheshire Cat assures Alice that everyone there is mad.
The famous nickname came from readers and later adaptations.
Myths and a manuscript's return.
One legend says Queen Victoria loved Alice and asked for Carroll's next book, receiving a dry mathematical treatise.
Carroll publicly denied this in 1896.
Another claim says the Hatter was inspired by hat makers poisoned by the mercury used on felt.
That poisoning was real, and the phrase mad as a hatter predates the book, but there is no evidence Carroll was making that point.
In 1928 Alice, by then Mrs Hargreaves, sold the manuscript at auction in London, and it went to the United States.
In 1948 American donors led by Luther Evans, the Librarian of Congress, bought and returned it to Britain in thanks for its wartime role.
It is now in the British Library.
The key idea: Alice began as a tale improvised on a rowing trip in 1862 for a ten-year-old girl who asked for it to be written down.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is the title 'first novel' disputed?
Answer. It depends on how you define a novel.
Question two. What set the stage for the ghost story contest that produced Frankenstein?
Answer. A volcanic eruption cooled the climate and kept the group indoors.
Question three. How did Dickens's childhood shape his novels?
Answer. Child labour after his father's imprisonment.
Question four. How did the story of Alice first come into being?
Answer. It was improvised aloud on a rowing trip.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
